market_context: United States; commercial or local honey stored at home
title: Why does honey crystallize, and is it still good?

seo.title: Why does honey crystallize, and can you still eat it?
seo.meta_description: Honey crystallization is a normal physical change, not a spoilage sign. Learn what causes it, how to liquefy honey gently, and what changes are more concerning.
seo.search_intent: Know why honey becomes grainy or solid, whether crystallized honey is safe, and how to make it liquid again.

excerpt: Honey can change from pourable to thick and grainy because some of its sugars form crystals. That is normal and does not, by itself, mean the honey has spoiled. Gentle warming can liquefy it again; persistent foam and a clearly fermented, alcoholic smell are different warning signs.
content_html:
You open a jar that has been sitting in the pantry and the honey no longer pours in a ribbon. It is pale, grainy, and almost spoon-solid. The obvious assumption is that it has gone bad. With honey, that is usually the wrong diagnosis. Crystallization is not the same as spoilage.

Honey is an unusually concentrated sugar solution

Most of honey is sugar dissolved in a relatively small amount of water, with glucose and fructose making up much of that sugar. The mixture can stay liquid for a long time, but it is not always permanently stable.

Over time, some glucose can leave the liquid phase and organize into crystals. Utah State University Extension describes honey as a supersaturated solution: enough sugar is dissolved that, under the right conditions, some eventually comes back out as solid crystals.

Why one jar crystallizes faster than another

Different honeys have different glucose-to-fructose ratios, and that strongly affects how readily they granulate. Tiny particles such as pollen or bits of wax in less-filtered honey can also provide starting points where crystals grow.

Temperature matters too. Penn State notes that refrigeration encourages crystallization, while Utah State describes temperatures around 57 °F (14 °C) as especially favorable for granulation. A jar in a cool pantry may therefore crystallize much sooner than another jar kept under different conditions.

Can you eat crystallized honey?

Yes. University extension guidance consistently treats crystallization as a natural process and says crystals themselves do not make honey unsafe.

In fact, creamed honey is made by deliberately controlling crystallization so that many small crystals create a smooth, spreadable texture. The difference is crystal size and structure, not “fresh honey” versus “bad honey.”

How to make it liquid again

If you prefer pourable honey, set the container in hot but not boiling water and warm it gradually until the crystals dissolve. Gentle stirring can help distribute the heat.

There is no need to boil honey. Excessive heat can darken it and alter aroma and flavor. If you only need a spoonful, warming a small portion also avoids repeatedly heating the whole jar.

What changes are more concerning?

Honey has little available water for many microorganisms, but fermentation can occur if its moisture level becomes high enough. Penn State advises discarding honey that foams and smells alcoholic, signs consistent with fermentation.

That looks and smells different from ordinary crystallization. Crystals make honey grainy, cloudy, or firm; fermentation may create gas, foam, and an abnormal fermented odor.

You generally do not need the refrigerator

For ordinary honey, a tightly closed container kept dry at a stable room temperature is usually more practical than refrigeration. The refrigerator is unnecessary for routine storage and can speed crystallization.

If your honey turns solid, the jar is not ruined. Eat it as-is—it spreads neatly and drips less—or warm it gently until it flows again. The texture change is physical; discard decisions depend on other signs.

faq.question: Is crystallized honey expired?
faq.answer: No. Crystallization is a normal physical process in honey and, by itself, does not mean the honey has spoiled.

faq.question: How do I make crystallized honey liquid again?
faq.answer: Warm the container gently in hot, not boiling, water until the crystals dissolve. Avoid unnecessary overheating.

faq.question: What does fermented honey look or smell like?
faq.answer: It may develop foam or gas and an alcoholic or fermented odor. Those signs are different from uniform sugar crystallization.
